title: Deploy Your First Prompt Flow in Azure AI Foundry
tagline: Compare prompt variants side by side instead of redeploying every tweak.
problemStatement: Teams shipping a customer-support bot need to iterate on prompt wording, test variants, and compare outputs before committing changes to production — doing this by editing raw strings in application code means every tweak requires a full redeploy and there's no structured way to compare two prompt versions side by side.
approachRationale: A raw prompt string embedded in application code would technically work, but it loses versioning, can't be A/B tested without custom tooling, and mixes prompt-engineering concerns with application logic. Azure AI Foundry's Prompt Flow gives you a visual, versioned flow with built-in variant comparison — the same underlying model call, but with iteration and evaluation built in rather than bolted on.
prerequisites: An Azure account with an active subscription (the free account's $200 starting credit fully covers this lab)
Access to an Azure AI Foundry project (create one at ai.azure.com if you don't have one)
Azure CLI 2.60+ installed and authenticated (`az login`)
learningObjectives: Create a Prompt Flow inside an Azure AI Foundry project
Wire a single LLM node to a deployed chat model
Add a second prompt variant and compare outputs side by side
Deploy the flow as a callable endpoint and invoke it from a Python client

steps.title: Open your Azure AI Foundry project
steps.instructions: Sign in at ai.azure.com and open (or create) a project. Note the project's endpoint URL from the Overview page — you'll need it in step 4.
steps.whyItMatters: A Foundry project is the scoping boundary for connected models, flows, and deployments — everything in this lab lives inside one project so cost and access can be managed together.
steps.expectedResult: The project Overview page loads and shows a non-empty Endpoint URL field.

steps.title: Create a new Prompt Flow
steps.instructions: In the left nav, select Prompt Flow → Create → Chat flow. Name it `support-bot-greeting`.
steps.whyItMatters: Chat flow (vs. a plain 'flow') pre-wires the conversation-history input, which is what you actually want for a support bot — starting from the right template avoids rebuilding that plumbing by hand.
steps.expectedResult: A new flow canvas opens with an `inputs`, an `llm` node, and an `outputs` node already connected.

steps.title: Connect the LLM node to a deployed chat model
steps.instructions: Click the `llm` node, and under Connection select an existing Azure OpenAI or Foundry model connection (create one under Management Center → Connections if none exists). Choose a small model such as gpt-4o-mini for this lab.
steps.whyItMatters: gpt-4o-mini keeps this lab in the free/low-cost tier — the concept (variant comparison) doesn't require a large model, and using a small one is the deliberate cost-conscious choice, not a limitation.
steps.expectedResult: The node shows a green connected indicator and the deployment name in its header.

steps.title: Write the base prompt
steps.instructions: In the llm node's prompt editor, write a system prompt for a support bot greeting, then click Run to test it against a sample chat_history input.
steps.whyItMatters: Testing one node in isolation before wiring the full flow catches prompt-formatting errors early — cheaper to fix here than after deployment.

code.snippet:
system:
You are a concise, friendly support assistant for {{product_name}}. Greet the user in one sentence and ask what they need help with.

steps.expectedResult: The Run panel shows a one-sentence greeting output, no error banner.

steps.title: Add a second prompt variant
steps.instructions: Click the three-dot menu on the llm node → Show variants → Add variant. Change the system prompt's tone to be more formal, and name it `variant_1_formal`.
steps.whyItMatters: This is the actual point of Prompt Flow over raw code: two variants living side by side, both versioned, both runnable — this is what lets you make an evidence-based choice instead of guessing which wording is better.
steps.expectedResult: Two variant tabs are now visible on the node, each independently runnable.

steps.title: Run both variants and compare
steps.instructions: Click Evaluate → select both variants → Submit with the same sample input for each.
steps.whyItMatters: Running identical input through both variants isolates the prompt wording as the only variable — without that control, you can't attribute a difference in output to the prompt change specifically.
steps.expectedResult: A comparison table shows both variants' outputs side by side.

steps.title: Deploy the flow as an endpoint
steps.instructions: Click Deploy at the top of the flow canvas. Choose a small instance size (Standard_DS2_v2 or the smallest available) and confirm.
steps.whyItMatters: Instance size directly drives hosting cost — the smallest size is sufficient for a lab-scale endpoint and keeps this deployment in the low-cost tier.
steps.expectedResult: A new endpoint appears under Deployments with status 'Succeeded' within a few minutes.

steps.title: Call the endpoint from Python
steps.instructions: Copy the endpoint URL and key from the Deployments page, then run the client snippet below.
steps.whyItMatters: Calling the deployed endpoint (not the design-time flow) confirms the thing you'd actually wire into a real application — the design-time Run button and the deployed endpoint are not the same code path.
steps.expectedResult: The script prints `200` and a JSON body containing the greeting text.

conceptChecks.question: If you wanted to compare three tones instead of two, what would change about how you evaluate them, and why would running all three against the exact same input still matter?
conceptChecks.answer: You'd add a third variant and run all three against the identical sample input in one Evaluate pass — the identical input is what isolates prompt wording as the only variable; adding a variant doesn't change that requirement, it just widens the comparison.

conceptChecks.question: Why does instance size matter here even though this is a low-traffic lab endpoint, and what would you check before choosing a larger size in a real deployment?
conceptChecks.answer: Cost scales with instance size regardless of traffic — an idle oversized endpoint still bills for capacity. In a real deployment you'd check expected concurrent request volume and latency requirements before sizing up, not default to a larger size preemptively.

validationChecklist: The flow canvas shows two variants on the llm node, both runnable without error
The Evaluate comparison table displays both variants' outputs for the same input
The Python client call returns HTTP 200 with a non-empty greeting string in the response body
cleanup: Delete the deployment: Deployments → support-bot-greeting deployment → Delete
Delete the flow (optional, no ongoing cost, but keeps the project tidy): Prompt Flow → support-bot-greeting → Delete
Confirm no orphaned compute instance remains under Management Center → Compute

costEstimate.freeTierNotes: Fully covered by the Azure free account's $200 starting credit if completed within a normal lab session and cleaned up afterward; gpt-4o-mini token costs for this lab's handful of test calls are a few cents at most.

relatedExams.why: AB-731 Domain 2 (Microsoft AI Apps & Services) covers Azure AI Foundry deployment patterns, which this lab exercises hands-on.
